item.title: Arizona's GOP keeps embracing election deniers who lose. It could happen again.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Election Day 2020 was fast approaching, and Alexander Kolodin wanted a spot inside the Arizona Republican Party's war room. Kolodin, an attorney who had lost a GOP primary for the state Senate that summer, was seen as something of a gadfly by some in the state GOP and hardly seen at all by others. But the Republicans running the show allowed him into an auxiliary war room on another floor of the hotel, distanced from the real action, one party leader recalled. People there "could say they were in the war room," he said. "If we needed something, then we'd call." Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Kolodin didn't wait to be summoned. On Election Day, complaints began flooding in about ballots marked with Sharpie markers. Soon, supporters of President Donald Trump were blaming Sharpies for what looked like a loss in Arizona. The Arizona Republican Party had investigated the matter and determined that Sharpies had not in fact caused problems. So its leaders were surprised when they learned that Kolodin was filing a lawsuit demanding that voters who used Sharpies be given a chance to vote again. The suit was filed the day after the election, the first of several challenges Kolodin championed over the 2020 results. Each failed in court, and they led to sanctions from the state bar association. But Kolodin's embrace of these claims catapulted him from a little-known attorney who badly lost his first campaign for office to a leading figure in Arizona politics and this year's Republican nominee for secretary of state. If he wins, he will be responsible for running the state's elections in 2028, when Arizona is expected to once again be a battleground in the presidential and Senate contests. Other election conspiracy theorists hold high office, but a victory here would mark the first time someone actively involved in attempting to subvert election results would be elected to run a state's elections. Arizona was a reliably Republican state just a decade ago, and then seen as a competitive battleground. But in recent years, the state GOP has repeatedly nominated candidates who have promoted Trump's false claims, only to see them lose in the general election. That includes Blake Master, who lost a Senate race in 2022, and Kari Lake, who lost races for governor in 2022 and Senate in 2024, even as Trump won the state. This fall, besides Kolodin, two other Republicans who acted to subvert the 2020 election results are also on the ballot: Andy Biggs for governor and Warren Petersen for attorney general. Some in the party predict a wipeout is coming and worry Democrats will consolidate and expand their power for years to come if Republicans continue this pattern. "The election denialists have dominated this party for six years," said one GOP strategist. "If we keep doing this, we will keep losing." Kolodin is not the only person who has advanced the lie that the 2020 election was stolen and is now running to oversee elections in a presidential battleground state. In Nevada, former state lawmaker Jim Marchant, the GOP nominee for secretary of state, claimed that both he and Trump were victims of election fraud in 2020 and says being called an election denier is a "badge of honor." In a recent interview, Anthony Forlini, Michigan's GOP nominee for secretary of state, wouldn't say who won the presidential election in 2020. "Everyone wants to trip up people on that whole question," he said. In Arizona, endorsing and promoting Trump's conspiracy theories were essential to Kolodin's rise. They brought him to the center of the action, drew admirers in the GOP base and won allies in powerful places. "Alex definitely stepped up when there were very few who could or would," said Tyler Bowyer, CEO of Turning Point USA. "He easily could have been, 'Nah, I'm not going to help.' No one would know who he was and he certainly wouldn't be running for secretary of state now." The cases increased Kolodin's public profile, but it came with a price, said Tyler Montague, president of the Arizona Public Integrity Alliance, a conservative think tank, who has known Kolodin for more than a decade and sometimes worked with him. "He found a path to notoriety and surrendered some of his political thinking to Trump, and that combination led him to where he's at," he said. "It's a cultlike mentality - uncritical acceptance of what the leader says. It's hard for him to get out of it because it's also the source of his status." After fighting for Trump following his 2020 loss, Kolodin was elected to the Arizona House in 2022. There, he earned a reputation as a fighter for ultraconservative principles, but also as an obstructionist who has incensed fellow Republicans as well as Democrats. Two GOP committee chairmen asked for him to be removed from their committees, three people familiar with the situation said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to candidly discuss a personnel matter. Kolodin did not respond to requests for comment or to a list of detailed questions. In other interviews, he has emphasized his support for election integrity, attacked his opponent's record and tried to downplay the events of 2020. "Election integrity has become the defining civil rights issue of our time," he wrote in a post on X thanking Trump for his endorsement. "We must protect the sanctity of every lawful vote, and we must restore confidence in our elections for every lawful voter, regardless of political party." Losses fuel a rising star Kolodin was raised in Arizona and returned to the state after earning a law degree at the University of Pennsylvania in 2013. He set up his own small law practice, taking a series of cases where he challenged government and election procedures, often on hot-button topics of public interest that landed in the news. Among them: He demanded public records in a sports arena deal. He tried to kill mask requirements in a public school district during the pandemic. And he worked to kick a congressional candidate off the ballot because of an error on her nominating petitions. Kolodin made his first run for political office in 2020, mounting a mostly self-funded primary campaign against a Republican incumbent for a state Senate seat. During that campaign, his opponent latched on to Kolodin's involvement in a 2014 defamation lawsuit where he represented a liberal activist who had collected and mailed a huge pile of filled-out ballots. Kolodin lost the case, and also badly lost the GOP primary. But he continued his work on election issues. That fall, he scored a victory in a dispute with Adrian Fontes, who at the time was running elections in Maricopa County, home to Phoenix and the state's largest county. Fontes had told voters that if they made a mistake marking their ballot, they could cross it out and fill in the proper oval. Kolodin's suit argued that this would open the door to allowing people who handle ballots to change votes after the fact. His suit forced a reversal by Fontes, a Democrat who is the current secretary of state and Kolodin's opponent this fall. But when Election Day arrived, his profile began to climb with his Sharpie lawsuit. The allegations, first voiced in remote corners of Twitter, were soon amplified by conservative mega-voices such as Charlie Kirk of Turning Point USA. By 10 a.m. the next day, there were 1,200 tweets per minute on Sharpies, one analysis found. Kolodin asked Montague, the conservative think tank president, if he would be a plaintiff in his Sharpie suit, Montague said. He declined, telling Kolodin there was nothing to these claims. The rumor was based on concerns that using a Sharpie marker would invalidate a ballot because the ink could bleed through and interfere with ballot marks on the other side of the paper. In fact, as the state GOP had discovered, the columns on the other side of the paper were aligned so that any bleed through would not impact other votes. Nonetheless, Kolodin "charged forward," Montague recalled. "He seemed to genuinely believe in the various conspiracy theories going on." One Republican attorney active in the party said Kolodin pursued the suit despite widespread opposition among Republican strategists in D.C. and Arizona. "It felt like he was trying to elbow his way into the conversation and, frankly, the limelight," he said. The case was quickly dismissed, but within weeks, Kolodin was back with another, more sweeping lawsuit, demanding that the election results be set aside due to "massive election fraud." The suit - one of several filed in states Joe Biden won - was conceived by national figures including Trump ally Sidney Powell, who promised these challenges would "release the kraken" and prove Trump actually won the election. She needed an attorney to carry the case, but no prominent Arizona election lawyer, including those who had worked for the Trump campaign and the Republican Party, would take the case, said three people familiar with the conversations inside GOP circles. Kolodin stepped in. "Most of the Republican attorneys saw the need to be as far away from this dumpster fire as you could possible get," said one of these people. "Were you to continue to pursue these cases you could be jeopardizing your law license." A federal judge found the allegations "sorely wanting of relevant or reliable evidence" and in December 2020, dismissed the case. Despite the courtroom setbacks, Kolodin was establishing himself as Arizona's go-to attorney when someone wanted to challenge election results. He represented Cyber Ninjas, which in 2021 ran a chaotic audit of 2020 ballots in Maricopa County (and ultimately found Biden's margin slightly bigger than official results indicated). In 2022, he represented a group that monitored ballot drop boxes and filmed people voting, claiming to be hunting for fraud. And his client list included people who falsely presented themselves as 2020 electors. In 2023, the State Bar of Arizona cited three lawsuits Kolodin filed, including the Sharpie suit, as it formally admonished him for violating his duty to the legal profession, the legal system and the public. The state bar sentenced him to 18 months of probation and required him to take five legal ethics courses. But while Kolodin was accumulating one loss after the next, his public profile was rising. In 2022, he again ran for the legislature, seeking a House seat representing Scottsdale, a suburb of Phoenix. His campaign material highlighted his role in many of these actions. And unlike in summer 2020, this time he won. 'Outrageous lies' Kolodin immediately made his mark in the Capitol, irritating people in both parties with unpredictable personal and legislative behavior, according to current and former lawmakers and others familiar with the situation. He became known for filing voluminous numbers of bills - 74 last year - and also for a proposal last year that would bar any legislator from introducing more than 10 bills per year. He backed a repeal of the ban on machine guns, silencers, sawed-off shotguns and pipe bombs. He was the only legislator of either party to vote against a "stolen valor" bill making it a crime to impersonate a veteran. (He said it would criminalize alleged lies by politicians, setting a dangerous precedent.) Several current and former GOP lawmakers described him as disruptive, unwilling to work with others and insistent on having things his way. Last year, he called any legislator, including some Republicans, who supported a particular version of a budget bill "an enemy of the people of Arizona." "He says things out loud that are nonsensical - objecting to motions, attempting to change procedure in a nonsensical way, outbursts in a heated debate on the floor," said one Republican who worked closely with Kolodin. His style, he said, is to "fly off the handle" and "shoot from the hip." On the campaign trail, Kolodin touts bipartisan successes, and in 2024, he helped reach a bipartisan elections reform package, which aligned post-election timelines for steps such as certification with new federal deadlines. But last year, he blew up chances for a bipartisan agreement with Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs's office on another elections measure by insisting on elements that the governor would never agree to - such as requirements making mail voting harder - and being unwilling to compromise, according to two people involved in the process. "He has particular views on certain issues and it's challenging to reason with him or find common ground," said Bo Dul, an Arizona election attorney who served as general counsel to Hobbs. "Often, those views are not grounded in fact or how election administration actually works and, as a result, he would often insist on positions that are just nonstarters." No deal was reached. Instead, the GOP legislature voted to put its proposal before voters this fall. If approved, it would, among other things, require mail-in voters - who make up about 80 percent of all voters in the state - to show identification. It's unclear how or where people voting by mail would be able to show ID. Kolodin has bemoaned failure to advance another election priority: requiring every voter to repeatedly verify their address to vote by mail. In an interview last year, he said that this reform could have helped increase Republican vote share in Arizona. "It could have flipped this state red for a generation. So I was just so incredibly disappointed to see it get killed," he told "The Jeff Oravits Show." Kolodin's panache for irritating his party and for advancing Trump's unfounded claims collided when a group of Arizona Republicans was criminally investigated, and then charged with conspiracy and fraud, for declaring themselves to be the state's representatives to the electoral college in 2020 when Biden actually won Arizona. In 2024, Kolodin, who represented some of these so-called fake electors, argued that the Arizona Republican Party's insurance policy should cover some of the electors' legal fees. He wrote the company that these people were officials of the Arizona Republican Party, according to a letter viewed by The Washington Post. The insurance company wound up paying out the policy's $1 million maximum toward their legal defense, documents show, some of which went to a law firm where Kolodin worked. In January 2026, then-Arizona Republican Party Chairwoman Gina Swoboda informed the party's executive committee that he had done this without consulting her or other party officers and that the result was a 10-fold hike in premiums. "We became aware of this matter in October 2025 when we inquired why our renewal premium was so high," she wrote. She said the party then made the "difficult but necessary decision" to drop coverage for 2026. That meant the officers of the party were vulnerable if they faced damages claims or lawsuits. This summer, Kolodin easily won the GOP primary for secretary of state, beating Swoboda, who had left her position as party chair earlier this year. He is running on election integrity, promising to implement "robust security protocols" and restore confidence in the elections system. But some in his party worry Kolodin's history of questioning election results could harm Republicans. "He is making outrageous lies about very important things related to the office that he is seeking," said Ken Bennett, a former Republican secretary of state and state senator in Arizona. "As long as the Republican Party nominates people who are too far to the right of the mainstream ... those nominees are going to have trouble in the general election," Bennett said of Kolodin. The events of 2020 loom large in Kolodin's race. During a spirited "candidates in conversation" on Arizona public television with his opponent, Kolodin was asked directly if he was an "election denier." "That's absurd," he replied. "I have one of the greatest bipartisan track records of working on elections issues of anybody in recent Arizona history." Pressed again as to whether he was an election denier, Kolodin answered, "No." Followed by reporters into the hallway after the event, he was asked directly if Trump won Arizona in 2020. "I think I answered that question," Kolodin replied. Asked again, Kolodin said, "Look, Joe Biden was the president. Congress said that Joe Biden won. Congress called the race." As for who won Arizona, Kolodin refused to say, asserting that he had already answered the question. After about a minute of this back and forth, the elevator arrived and Kolodin stepped in. Reporters kept pressing: Was the ballot count in Maricopa County accurate? "It's time for us to go," Kolodin replied. He insisted again that he had already answered, and the elevator doors closed. item.title: 6 takeaways from often contentious South Carolina Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
US Senate candidates Democrat Annie Andrews and Republican Sen. Darline Graham take notes before a debate in Columbia, South Carolina, on October 11. - Sam Wolfe/Reuters South Carolina has emerged as perhaps the most surprising Senate race to be competitive late in the 2026 midterm elections. And on Sunday night, appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham, Democrat Annie Andrews and Libertarian nominee Kasie Whitener took part in the only debate currently scheduled in the race. The debate was often contentious, with both Graham and Andrews taking aim at each other. Andrews focused on the idea that Graham — the late former Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister, whom President Donald Trump plucked from obscurity to succeed him — is the choice of political insiders and not running a serious campaign. She at one point alluded to an embarrassing moment at a primary runoff debate in which Graham said, “National security is not my thing.” “If your surgeon said that appendectomies aren’t really his thing, would you still hand him a scalpel? No,” Andrews said. “So why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the US Senate? She is unserious and unqualified.” Graham also hit Andrews early and often, seeking to tie her to the political left. And she repeatedly took offense to the attacks that Andrews lodged, accusing Andrews of going after her family. Below are some takeaways from the debate. Graham avoided another major flub Job No. 1 for Graham was avoiding a moment like the one on national security. And she cleared that bar. At that GOP debate against Rep. Ralph Norman, she was asked a relatively basic — at least for a senator — question about US foreign policy interests in Taiwan and the South China Sea. Seemingly not knowing where to go with it, she just admitted that she didn’t know much about the issue. At the same debate, she also mistakenly cited 50 million people living in South Carolina, when the actual number is less than 6 million. That doesn’t mean Sunday was smooth sailing. Graham paused awkwardly at times. She struggled to make some of her attack lines, such as on transgender rights, land. Some of her claims — like that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon before the US and Israel launched the war earlier this year — don’t actually appear true. But for a Republican running in a pretty red state, she came across as more capable than before. Republican Sen. Darline Graham reacts before a debate with Senate candidates Democrat Annie Andrews and Libertarian Kasie Whitener in Columbia, South Carolina, on October 11. - Sam Wolfe/Reuters Graham came out swinging That being said, Graham seemed to confirm that her campaign is quite concerned about Andrews, judging by how much time she spent attacking the Democrat. It started almost instantly, with Graham calling Andrews “most radical liberal that’s ever run for state office in South Carolina” in her first answer. She accused Andrews of supporting government-run healthcare, which Andrews denied. She pointed to Andrews’ past work on gun control issues. She attacked Andrews for opposing President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and for having the support of Jane Fonda’s political action committee. And after Andrews mentioned her primary runoff debate moment, Graham accused her of lying about her liberal positions. “Let’s talk about what’s not your thing. Your thing, apparently, is not being honest with the people of South Carolina. At least I’m honest. If I don’t know something, I am glad to say it, and I’ll say it again tonight,” she said. “But you are deceiving the people of South Carolina. You have flip-flopped on everything. There’s so many social media posts out there to prove different. Shame on you.” The attacks confirmed the competitiveness of the race. The national GOP recently turned heads by spending $5 million to shore up Graham’s campaign. US Senate candidate Democrat Annie Andrews arrives for a debate with candidates Republican Darline Graham and Libertarian Kasie Whitener in Columbia, South Carolina, on October 11. - Sam Wolfe/Reuters Andrews distanced herself from the Democratic Party and the left But Andrews had a pretty memorable answer for much of it. “She’s been told to come out here and call me Bernie Ocasio Mamdani; that’s what’s in her script,” Andrews said, referring to a trio of democratic socialist lawmakers. “But the truth is: My name is Annie Andrews, and there shouldn’t be any confusion about that because, unlike my opponent, I haven’t changed my name recently.” Graham opted not to use her married name — Darline Graham Nordone — when she was appointed as a senator. “My legal name is Graham and has always been Graham,” she said. “And you know why it’s Graham? Because I lost my parents when I was a little girl, and I kept the name Graham so that I felt connected to them.” At another point in the debate, Andrews said that “both parties have failed on immigration” and that “Democrats have failed on the border.” Andrews added: “And the truth is, I support the Second Amendment. I believe we need a secure border, and we need to deport illegal immigrants who break the law, and yes, I want to lower taxes on the middle class.” Graham tries to make transgender attacks land Few attacks have been as central to the race as the GOP’s efforts to focus on transgender issues. Just in the last week, Trump posted on social media using an anti-transgender slur for Andrews, and Andrews launched a direct-to-camera ad defending herself on the issue. But if you blinked, you might have missed it Sunday night. Graham brought it up twice, but only briefly. And she did so both times at the end of an answer, right before the debate quickly moved on. That included at the very end of the debate. “But let’s talk about a couple of other concerns I have — that she’s deceiving the people of South Carolina with these transgender issues,” Graham said in the final words of the night. The debate moderator quickly signaled the debate had to end there, and it was over. That was a win for Andrews, in that she didn’t really have to answer for the issue — or explain her 2022 comments on social media calling a state law banning transgender athletes from playing on girls’ and women’s sports teams at public schools “shameful.” Graham defended the Iran war Andrews repeatedly pointed to Graham declining to vote with Democrats and a few Republicans to bringing the Iran war to an end, noting Graham has had three chances to do so. Graham responded by claiming that Iran nearly had a nuclear weapon — which is not backed up by known US intelligence. But unlike some GOP Senate candidates who have said the war needs to end, she went a little further in defending the need to give Trump more time. She argued Iran is being strangled financially. “Why in the world would we stop now when they are still dangerous and we are close to ending the war?” Graham said. “Again, I think the president wants to end the war. I know he does. We all want the war to end. But I support a strong military. I believe in peace through strength.” US Senate candidate Democrat Annie Andrews takes notes before a debate with Republican US Sen. Darline Graham and US Senate Libertarian candidate Kasie Whitener in Columbia, South Carolina, on October 11. - Sam Wolfe/Reuters Few mentions of Trump Few things loomed as large over the debate as Trump; his unpopularity is a major reason South Carolina and other deep-red states are as competitive this fall. But he wasn’t a major focus. There was the occasional mention of something Trump has done, but he wasn’t really a focal point for anybody. In fact, the word “Trump” was only uttered a handful of times. Graham mentioned the president just a few times, praising him for creating an AI task force and waiving restrictions on red-dye diesel . Even when Andrews was arguing Graham was the pick of insiders, she didn’t actually cite the one insider above all who elevated Graham: Trump. And when talking about the war, she generally didn’t attach it to the president. That perhaps shouldn’t be too surprising from the Democrat. While Trump is broadly unpopular nationwide, this is still a state he won by 18 points in 2024. item.title: Newsom typically relishes battling Trump — except on undocumented students
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Gavin Newsom has rarely shied away from a fight with Donald Trump, especially over immigration. He didn’t hesitate last year to sign into law a ban on federal immigration agents wearing masks in the state. And when he put his name on a package of legislation this year further clamping down on immigration enforcement, he said he was doing so to “push back on Trump’s Orwellian immigrant tactics.” But when it came to a bill that would have required the state’s public universities and community colleges to make undocumented immigrant students eligible for campus employment, Newsom balked. Trump officials, he wrote in a message explaining his veto last month, are “quick to wreak destruction for political spectacle.” The risk of them seeking retribution against the schools was too great. Newsom’s decision to avoid confrontation prolongs a yearslong student-led push to persuade skeptical university officials to enact a first-in-the-nation policy that would benefit the roughly 60,000 undocumented students enrolled in the three school systems. And it has deflated immigrant rights activists in his home state ahead of Newsom's likely presidential run. “There’s disappointment that on this issue, the governor hasn't been willing to take a risk for a very important part of the California population,” said Maria Blanco, the former executive director of the UC Immigrant Legal Services Center. “Even in a progressive state like California, immigration sometimes still continues to be this third rail, especially if you're running for president.” The governor’s unwillingness to force the issue with Trump stemmed, at least in part, from what he said in his veto message was a concern that the hiring requirement wouldn’t hold up under legal scrutiny since federal law prohibits employers from hiring undocumented workers. Asked for comment, a spokesperson for Newsom referred to the governor’s veto message. Advocates for the idea that students living in the country illegally should be permitted to work campus jobs have relied heavily on a legal theory a group of UCLA law professors published in 2022 that argued the federal ban doesn’t apply to state agencies. The theory was enough to spur discussion among the UC Board of Regents, which considered implementing a policy allowing the hires, but ultimately punted on the idea in 2024. Rich Leib, the chair of the regents at the time who had signaled support for hiring undocumented students, said that enthusiasm on the board waned after three "established" law firms said they would not defend the university if its policy was challenged in court. With a second Trump term looming, Leib said a majority of the regents, including him, decided the timing was not right to challenge an administration that could be hostile to immigrants and voted to table the issue. They were particularly concerned, he said, about the possibility that immigration officials might be able to gain access to personal data about undocumented students on the university payroll. “It was the most emotional experience I had as a regent because it brought you to people who were directly negatively affected by it,” Leib said, referring to students who protested at the board meeting following the vote to shelve the plan. “These are people who have done really well their whole lives. They worked really hard to get where they did, and now you're telling them they can't get a job.” Joel Raznick, a regent emeritus who also voted for the delay, said that the possibility of Trump returning to the White House was “certainly on my mind.” Raznick, who emphasized he was not speaking on behalf of the UC, said he had been concerned about the possibility the Trump administration would respond to the hiring policy by cutting federal funding to the university – a tactic it has used in other fights with the UC – and that undocumented students could be “readily identified and deported.” “I thought that we were doing a better service for undocumented students at that moment by preserving the university's ability to operate,” Raznick said. “Because those risks are real, as we now know.” Anna Markowitz, president of the UCLA Faculty Association, which advocated for the hiring policy, pushed back on that rationale. “Who are we allowing to suffer by claiming that we’re saving the institution?” she asked. Omar Rodriguez, a spokesperson for the UC, said that the university’s “evaluation of this important issue is ongoing.” He pointed out that the UC remained neutral on the bill Newsom vetoed. “UC has been a leader in supporting undocumented students, who are vital members of the UC community and make significant contributions to our economy and society as scholars, researchers, and future leaders,” Rodriguez said. Along with the UC, the legislation would have applied to the California State University and community college systems. In statements, spokespeople for both systems said they also did not come out for or against the bill and support undocumented students while complying with state and federal laws. Immigration advocates criticize Newsom and the regents for what they see as their overly cautious approach. Having a law on the books, they argue, would provide a layer of protection for the school systems if they were to have a policy allowing undocumented students to work on campus. They also point to a ruling in a state appeals court last year that found the UC’s adherence to federal law forbidding employment was discriminatory. The ruling stated that the university could not rely on fear of federal retaliation as a reason for not adopting a more permissive stance, and ordered it to “reconsider its policy based on proper criteria.” “They're really caught in between a rock and a hard place,” said Ahilan Arulanantham, a UCLA law professor who helped write the 2022 legal theory. “They have to comply with the state court decision, and they're not going to get the benefit of any California legislation protecting them from above.” The ruling, though, did not require the university to change its policy and did not include a deadline for the UC to comply. “Large institutions tend to be risk adverse,” Blanco said. “And I don't think this is a climate where the UC would affirmatively go do this and then wait to be sued.” This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/11/newsom-veto-student-jobs-trump-01113178

item.title: 6 senators call for White House to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.” Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. “The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS's “Face the Nation.” He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. “This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said. Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump. Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, noted that the total amount of diesel appears to be less than what the U.S. uses in a day. Nephew argued that Iran and Russia might benefit more than the U.S. “The Iranians are probably very excited because it shows that there’s a lot of pressure still on the U.S. And the Russians are excited because it puts a big hole in the sanctions regime,” he said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices. —- Associated Press writer Mae Anderson in New York contributed to this report. item.title: 1 person dies in new attack on Saudi airport, a day after Houthi strike kills 13
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jana Choukeir, Maha El Dahan, Timour Azhari and Yasmine Ghania DUBAI/RIYADH, Oct 11 (Reuters) - One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified ‌projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. Eleven people were wounded in addition to the fatality, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. Coalition forces also said Saudi ‌air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country's Eastern Province, and a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait had been intercepted. Emergency alerts were ​also issued in Abha, in the south, early on Monday but the danger had since passed, the Saudi Civil Defense said. The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis, who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in. The airport was closed after the attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in ‌more than a decade. HOUTHIS CLAIM RESPONSIBILITY FOR OTHER ATTACKS In a televised speech ⁠on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and said the group had also struck the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco. The Saudi government's media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment. The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike ⁠on Dammam's King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that "damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way." An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammam told Reuters that around 8:30 p.m. (1730 GMT) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave. Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and departures at Dammam airport, ​the ​kingdom's third-largest. The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings ​seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said. Britain's embassy ‌in Saudi Arabia in a post on X advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Medina. US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom. 'WORSE IS YET TO COME,' HOUTHIS WARN Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah television. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining ‌Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and ​Israel launched in February. In a post on Telegram, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said he told his Saudi counterpart that Tehran ​was ready to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen. ENERGY CONFERENCE STILL GOING AHEAD A five-day conference ​of international energy organization WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention centre about 10 km (6 miles) from the Riyadh airport, the Saudi energy ministry said. A ‌ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead, according to a media ​advisory from the ministry. It was not clear which ​ministers attended. Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link. German officials were trying to organise a return flight for economy minister Katherina Reiche. She was supposed to return to Berlin from Riyadh on Monday but the ministry said it appeared likely her flight would be unable to take off. Separately, Saudi authorities announced that in-person ​classes at schools in Riyadh would be shifted to remote learning from Sunday ‌until Thursday. Sunday's attack brought the death toll in attacks on Riyadh's airport to 18 for the week. In Saturday's attack, the dead included four Saudis while the remainder were foreign ​nationals, Saudi authorities said. (Reporting by Jana Choukeir and Maha El Dahan in Dubai, Timour Azhari Riyadh, Menna Alaa El-Din and Yasmine Ghania in Cairo, James Mackenize and Sarah El Safty; ​Writing by Jan Wolfe and Patricia Zengerle; Editing by Andrew Mills, Gareth Jones, Edmund Klamann and Lincoln Feast.) item.title: Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says Democrats are on the verge of retaking the House
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries expressed growing confidence that his party will regain control of the House in November , as he visited two battleground districts in recent days to help Democratic candidates unseat Republican incumbents. Jeffries campaigned Friday in New Jersey's competitive 7th Congressional District alongside Democratic challenger Rebecca Bennett, a Navy veteran seeking to unseat Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. The following day, he traveled to Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District to rally with Democrat Bob Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner challenging Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick. The two districts are heavily suburban, fairly affluent and politically divided — and they've caused heartburn for Democrats in recent years. The moderate Fitzpatrick has a long history of outrunning other Republicans and winning crossover support since he was first elected in 2016. Control of Kean's seat has flipped twice since 2018, but he narrowly won a competitive reelection two years ago. Democrats have invested in both races this year and view both of them as highly competitive, as they hope to take advantage of an unfavorable political environment for President Trump's party. "We're running through the finish line. We take nothing for granted, but we're on the verge of taking back control of the House of Representatives," Jeffries told reporters following Saturday's event in Pennsylvania. In a briefing with a small group of political reporters Wednesday, Jeffries pointed to a handful of districts in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and New York as opportunities for Democrats. He also said he plans to visit two South Texas districts. Republicans control the House by a single-digit margin, so the outcome of the midterms could be decided by a fairly small number of races. Jeffries declined to predict how many seats his party could gain in November. "I'm very confident that we're going to take back the majority, but it remains to be seen what that looks like in terms of the number of seats that we pick up, which is going to depend on the conditions that exist over the next few weeks," he said in the briefing. During the rally in Bucks County, a perennial swing county that supported Mr. Trump by a razor-thin margin in 2024 after years of narrow Democratic victories, Harvie said: "It is not an accident that Hakeem Jeffries is here tonight." "He knows what we're going to do with this district. He knows the potential," he said. Fitzpatrick's campaign told CBS News that the Republican lawmaker "is aware of Hakeem's visit, he still considers him a friend, and he looks forward to working with him in a bipartisan manner in the 120th Congress." "Leader Jeffries is doing what he needs to do, and Brian completely understands that," the campaign's statement continued. Fitzpatrick, who is seeking a sixth term, has cultivated a moderate image and put distance between himself and Mr. Trump, voting with House Democrats to rescind tariffs on Canada and restrict the Iran war. He also voted against final passage of the Trump administration's signature "Big, Beautiful Bill" last year. Most recently, he pushed back last week on the president's plan to buy diesel from Russia. Democrats have argued Fitzpatrick hasn't consistently opposed the president's agenda, pointing to an earlier vote in favor of the "Big, Beautiful Bill." Fitzpatrick has said he voted against the final legislation after the Senate added steeper Medicaid cuts. Judi Reiss, a Democratic local elected official in Lower Makefield Township, Pennsylvania, told CBS News at Saturday's rally with Jeffries and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro that she has "no personal animosity toward [Fitzpatrick] whatsoever, but he hasn't done anything. He's been a rubber stamp for Donald Trump." "He has not been independent, and it's very disappointing," said Reiss, who sought the 2020 Democratic nomination for Fitzpatrick's seat but dropped out before the primary. Still, Fitzpatrick has survived on challenging terrain in the past — and overperformed other Republicans. Vice President Kamala Harris narrowly won his district in 2024, but Fitzpatrick won reelection the same year by a more than 12-point margin. The Cook Political Report rated the Pennsylvania district "Leans Republican" on Friday, down from its previous "Likely Republican" assessment. Bucks County resident Bill Craig, a Republican who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick, told CBS News he believes Harvie has a "slim chance" of winning the district, but he expects the race to be close due to heavy Democratic turnout. "Brian Fitzpatrick could cure cancer right now, and they still wouldn't vote for him," Craig said. "He's very middle-of-the-road. They're trying to paint him as some kind of MAGA psycho." Jeffries visited Fitzpatrick's district a day after campaigning for Bennett across the Delaware River, in a New Jersey seat that the Cook Political report sees as Democratic-leaning — a shift after it called the race a toss-up as recently as last month . The GOP incumbent there, Kean, is seeking a third term representing a district that stretches from the New York City suburbs to the Pennsylvania border, with Mr. Trump's Bedminster golf club sitting in the middle. He was first elected after the district was made slightly redder in 2022, and defeated Democratic Rep. Tom Malinowski. House Speaker Mike Johnson also campaigned with Kean in recent weeks. Jeffries' campaign stops illustrate the importance of suburban congressional districts that could help determine which party controls the House next year. In last week's briefing with reporters, the Democratic leader described all four competitive Republican-held districts in Pennsylvania as Democratic pickup opportunities. In addition to Fitzpatrick's seat, Democrats are targeting a northeastern Pennsylvania district and two seats in eastern and central Pennsylvania. He also singled out the race in New York's 17th Congressional District, where Democrat Cait Conley is challenging Republican Rep. Mike Lawler. Jeffries to campaign in South Texas races Meanwhile, Democrats are defending two competitive districts in South Texas, and have signaled they plan to go on offense in two GOP-held districts in the region. Republicans made substantial gains among Latinos in 2024 , especially in South Texas, where some counties that were once Democratic strongholds became light-red. Jeffries argued that Latino voters could swing back to Democrats, pointing to concerns over the cost of living and the Trump administration's aggressive immigration policies. He said the political environment has changed dramatically in the Rio Grande Valley, where Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez are seeking reelection. Jeffries said he also plans to campaign in the coming weeks for two Texas Democrats who hope to unseat Republicans. Tejano music star Bobby Pulido is running against Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in a toss-up district , and Democrat Johnny Garcia is challenging Republican nominee Carlos De La Cruz in a seat that's viewed as redder . The Democratic leader also rejected the notion that newly drawn Republican congressional maps in Texas and Florida would deliver the substantial gains GOP strategists had initially anticipated. "Under no circumstances are Republicans winning five seats in Texas or four seats in Florida," Jeffries told CBS News last week. The National Republican Congressional Committee has disputed Democrats' increasingly optimistic assessments of the battleground map, pointing to Republican campaign resources and ground game efforts in competitive districts. If Democrats regain control of the House, Jeffries would be positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House in American history. While the party that doesn't control the White House almost always performs well in the midterms, the exact result is tougher to predict. In the 2022 midterms, when Republicans were buoyed by former President Joe Biden's unpopularity, predictions of a sweeping GOP wave failed to materialize. Republicans narrowly won control of the House but failed to recapture the Senate until two years later. Asked by CBS News whether Democrats risk that kind of election night disappointment, Jeffries acknowledged the outcome will depend on the political climate and spending. He said that while the current environment appears favorable to Democrats, the amount of money being spent by Republican-aligned political groups could ultimately limit the number of seats his party gains. House Republicans' campaign committee had more cash on hand than the group's Democratic counterpart at the end of August. Jeffries disputed suggestions that Republicans hold an overwhelming financial advantage in House battlegrounds, arguing that Democrats are effectively at parity when spending by candidates, committees and outside groups is considered together. On the GOP side, Johnson is also barnstorming frontline districts as Republicans fight to maintain their majority — and look for opportunities to unseat vulnerable Democrats. Johnson said the other day he expects to visit about 40 districts this month. In recent days, Johnson has visited Michigan and Pennsylvania with incumbent Republicans, and campaigned alongside two Iowa Republicans who are aiming to retain GOP-held districts: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Joe Mitchell. He also campaigned last week in Ohio with Derek Merrin, who is hoping to unseat longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur in a toss-up district. It's a rematch of 2024, when Merrin lost to Kaptur by around 2,400 votes . During his visit to Ohio, Johnson said he expects control of the House to be determined by at least 22 seats that he sees as "jump-balls." He has expressed optimism that Republicans can retain their majority. "This will come down to the outcome of about 22 districts around the country, and I believe we can win those," Johnson told reporters late last month. Mr. Trump has also continued an aggressive campaign schedule aimed at boosting Republican candidates. Jeffries said he welcomes his increased involvement. "The more Donald Trump campaigns for Republicans across the country, the better for the opportunity for Democrats to further convince the American people that we actually are the only ones determined to make life more affordable for them," Jeffries said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jeffries-democrats-control-house-battleground-races/

McConnell said the ICE agent allegedly was pursuing the man and another person in their car and during the chase, the driver and the passenger left their vehicle on foot. KTRK - PHOTO: Law enforcement officials are at the scene after a man was struck by a vehicle driven by an ICE agent during chase, according to the Harris Courty Sheriff's Office, on Oct. 10, 2026, in Harris County, Texas. "We're here to investigate the crash," he told reporters. Deputies were collecting video evidence from nearby buildings as part of their investigation, McConnell said. No arrests have been made. Mendoza-Cervantes was not found as of Sunday afternoon, ICE said. Man fatally shot by federal officer in Houston was not ICE target, DHS says Family members of Parra-Hernandez, community leaders and officials of the immigration FIEL Houston held a news conference in Houston on Sunday. "We have been in contact with Miguel’s family, and they are very worried about his health. Espinosa demanded accountability from ICE and called for a transparent investigation of the incident. "We have more questions than answers. The biggest question we have is why does this keep happening? We demand answers and transparency from all agencies involved," Espinosa said. Harris County Precinct 4 Commissioner Lesley Briones called on ICE to provide all evidence to the Harris County Sheriff's office and to cooperate with the investigation, adding that she was "horrified" about the incident. item.title: He shares a name with a Cornell rape suspect. Strangers started hunting him down.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The messages told him he should “rot in hell” and be thrown in jail. His friends and family received a barrage of menacing threats. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Strangers found his cellphone number and peppered his phone with abusive texts. His face was plastered across angry videos online. Even TMZ called him. The messengers had wrongly concluded that the man was one of the seven Chi Phi fraternity members accused of participating in a 2024 gang rape at Cornell University, a case that has commanded public attention since the accuser, known as “Jane Doe,” filed a civil lawsuit last month. But the man, a graduate student in engineering at the University of Pennsylvania, never attended Cornell - he merely shares a first and last name with one of the accused men. To make matters clear, he recently changed his LinkedIn bio to read, “I do NOT go to Cornell.” As the Cornell case has fueled public debate, it has inspired a frenzy of online sleuths, who are racing to identify and expose personal information about Jane Doe and the men she has accused, a phenomenon called “doxing.” Since Jane Doe filed the lawsuit, she has faced death threats and been confronted at her home by armed police after someone made a false report, an action called swatting, according to Thomas Giuffra, her attorney. In their rush, the digital vigilantes have made errors - falsely identifying a slew of people who are not connected to the case. At least three other women have been misidentified as Jane Doe on social media, Giuffra said, prompting a wave of videos in which women declare, “I am Jane Doe,” to show solidarity with the accuser and attempt to obscure her identity. After the home address of a Marine Corps sergeant who shares a name with one of the accused was mistakenly added to court documents, his family received threats, said John Manly, an attorney representing his family. The error led the New York Supreme Court judge handling the case to seal several court documents Friday and to condemn the harassment as “brash, reckless, and ultimately dangerous internet vigilantism.” The Penn grad student said he has been worried that online vigilantes might find his home address, adding that “overall, the past few weeks have taken a toll on my mental health.” The men accused in the Cornell case have not been charged, and The Washington Post is not naming them. One man who shares a name with one of the accused, and who graduated from Cornell four years before the incident, posted a video showing messages he had received. “You can’t hide. Your future is over. You’ll get exactly what you deserve, which is prison,” one said. In another video, he read a message from a woman claiming to be a witch who said she placed a hex on him: “Your soul will not find peace for the rest of your life,” she had told him. The Marine sergeant’s mother said she and her family have been “absolutely terrorized with threats.” She said her son has received a torrent of hateful messages through social media, while she and her daughter have received phone calls and text messages, including in the middle of the night. One person said, “I will find you.” Another said, “Rope is cheap and gravity is free.” The mother said that they’ve tried to tell people they had the wrong person, but that people just called them liars. People have also thrown garbage and unidentified substances in their yard, she said, including what looked like dog poop. She said it has been hard for the family to sleep. “We really - I can’t stress this enough - we really want to be left alone.” For years, online sleuths have misidentified the subjects of high-profile news events, according to University of Michigan professor Sarita Schoenebeck, who studies online harassment. A Brown University student who had been missing when pressure-cooker bombs detonated near the Boston Marathon finish line in 2013 was falsely named as the bomber by online sleuths. He had died by suicide a month before the bombing, but he was elevated as a possible suspect in the fallout. Schoenebeck said the damage to people named by mistake can persist long after people point out the errors. “Once misinformation spreads, corrections rarely reach as many people as the original claims,” she said. There are few reliable statistics on the frequency of doxing, but Schoenebeck said people turn to such methods when “they believe the justice system has failed. However, doxing itself lacks the fact-finding, safeguards and accountability that an effective justice system requires.” There is no comprehensive national law that prohibits posting someone’s personal information. Some states bar people from publishing addresses or other information with the intent to harass or harm someone. A federal law also makes it a crime to share sensitive information about certain federal officials, jurors and others to threaten, intimidate or incite violence. Some bystanders have targeted people more distantly connected to the Cornell case. While at least two websites feature the names and photos of the accused, a longer list of fraternity members has also appeared online. “It wasn’t just seven. 50 other individuals knew what was happening and did NOTHING,” one post on Facebook reads. It includes pictures of Chi Phi fraternity members. Some of the online posts have included former members who graduated before the incident and were not part of a group chat involving the accused, and who are now facing harassment, their attorney, Adam Ford, wrote to Cornell’s general counsel in a letter reviewed by The Post. Ford said his clients have received death threats and hate mail, with some facing adverse consequences from their universities and employers, such as being put on leave. These alumni “had nothing to do with the events surrounding Jane Doe,” Ford wrote in the letter. “Nevertheless, they are being wrongfully accused on social media of having involvement.” The letter was first reported by CBS News. In his letter, Ford asked Cornell to provide letters to the alumni verifying that they were not part of the incident and to call on the public to stop harassing current and former members of the fraternity. Cornell declined to comment on the letter to The Post, citing pending litigation. The Penn student said he understands the human impulse to seek justice. “I salute those who are willing and strong enough to take matters into their own hands, especially when large organizations and institutions take too long to address an issue,” he told The Post. However, he said that his case demonstrates that it’s more important than ever to fact-check sources and verify information. “Mob mentality is real, and it can spread just as easily on social media,” he said. “People just need to be mindful of the impact our words and actions can have.” CORRECTION: A man who shares a name with one of the accused posted a video saying he graduated from Cornell four years before the incident. An earlier version of this article mistakenly said it was two years prior. item.description:

Angelina Stone and her loved ones were identified as victims of the shooting that occurred at a home in Erie, Pa. around 5 p.m. local time on Friday, Oct. 9, according to CBS News . The news outlet reported that Stone was just four days from giving birth. The victims also included her two children, brothers and a friend. Family friend Lisa Simmers told CBS News, “Her two babies were on the spectrum. Innocent children, couldn’t have told on that man if they wanted to, and he still killed them.” She added, “It’s mind-blowing to me to understand what was happening in that house while we were standing outside. The feeling of helplessness and knowing we couldn’t do anything and she was right there.” Perry Street in Erie, Pa. Credit: Google Simmers told Erie News Now that Stone had a “beautiful” family. “She was pregnant, about to have her baby in a couple of days. She had a daughter that was almost two, and her son Isiah, who I believe was like four or five, and they were all just beautiful. Beautiful children. And definitely did not deserve what happened to them,” the friend said. A GoFundMe has been created to raise funds for Stone and her children’s funeral arrangements. The fundraiser identifies Stone’s children as son Isiah, daughter Amari’anna and unborn baby Kyrie. “We have no finances ready to cover this loss, and we have only two weeks from today to get everything done. The funds from this fundraiser will go toward funeral expenses and the fees related to their final arrangements so they can be sent off correctly. This is more than our family can carry alone right now, and we truly need the community to rally around us,” the description for the fundrasier reads. PEOPLE reached out to the Erie County Sheriff’s Office on Sunday, Oct. 11, but did not immediately hear back. A press release on Saturday, Oct. 10 stated that police arrived on the scene within minutes of receiving the alert. The nine deaths occurred before officers arrived, according to the investigation. There were no additional gunshots after police arrived. “Our hearts remain with the victims, their loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss of life,” the City of Erie said in the release. Chief of Police Richard Lorah later said in a press conference that police found two deceased females outside the residence within minutes of arriving. “Video evidence reviewed by investigators shows those two women arriving at the residence, hearing distress, seeking assistance from neighbors and pounding on the door. The audio video also appears to capture muffled gunfire from inside the residence before the suspect emerged and fatally shot both women,” he said. Based on evidence so far, investigators believe that the suspect died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The nine dead individuals included eight family members and one family friend. Lorah also stated that one of the victims was “eight months pregnant.” Victims included a 51-year-old female and a 37-year-old female found outside the residence; a 5-year-old boy and a 1-year-old girl were found on the first floor, and a 24-year-old female, a 44-year-old female, a 19-year-old male and a 21-year-old male on the second floor and stairwell. The suspected shooter, a 45-year-old, was found dead on the second floor with a firearm. “Some scenes some scenes stay with you long after you leave them. Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Luc Cohen Oct 11 (Reuters) - A US judge on Sunday blocked the Trump administration from using taxpayer money to pay for political advertisements, after ‌publicly funded television ads glorifying US President Donald Trump began airing in ‌late September and sparked a bipartisan backlash. Manhattan-based US District Judge Jennifer Rochon temporarily barred the advertisements after ​plaintiffs including watchdog group Common Cause brought a lawsuit alleging the ads were political propaganda designed to help Republican candidates in the November 3 midterm elections, not public service announcements. The Trump administration was already planning to stop running the ads before Rochon's order, ‌according to a separate statement ⁠filed with the court on Saturday. The decision caps days of controversy over the taxpayer-funded advertisements, which were aired in the final weeks ⁠before the midterm elections. “We won’t stop until this administration is held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste and abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again," said ​Common ​Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomón. Trump on ​Monday said he considered the ‌ads to be a "positive promotion for our great U.S.A." but that they would no longer be funded by taxpayers, and the White House said this week that the president's political action committee, MAGA PAC, would fund the ads going forward. The White House said Trump's political action committee will not reimburse taxpayers for the ads that have already ‌run. The ads end with a disclaimer saying they ​were paid for by the US government. The ​Justice Department did not immediately respond ​to a request for comment about the judge's order. The plaintiffs, which ‌also included a public employee union ​and a candidate for ​Alabama state representative, had asked Rochon to temporarily block the ads by Friday so that they could not air during weekend programming such as football games and ​Saturday Night Live. Democratic Party ‌officials also challenged the ads in a separate suit brought in federal court ​in Washington. (Reporting by Luc Cohen; Additional reporting by Courtney Rozen in Washington; ​Editing by Clarence Fernandez and Stephen Coates) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-judge-orders-halt-taxpayer-235125025.html
